name: Ayesha Memon (fictional)
setting: Hyderabad, Sindh (simulated) - urban, Latifabad; university student
presenting: Sudden surges of fear before class presentations: racing heart, shaking hands, breathlessness and a strong urge to leave the room. She walked out of a presentation last week and now dreads the next one.
background: Second-year BS student living with her parents and two younger brothers. Good grades until this semester, when presentations became graded. A friend persuaded her to book the session.
culturalNote: Speaks Urdu at university and Sindhi at home. Her father frames ghabrahat (nervousness) as weakness to be overcome with study and prayer. Respect the family's faith as a resource rather than positioning therapy against it.

n1.client: Assalam-o-alaikum. My friend made me come. Before every presentation my heart races so hard I think something is wrong with me.

options.text: Thank you for coming even though it wasn't your idea. Could you walk me through what happens in those moments, from the start?
options.feedback: Open question (OARS: O). It invites the client to tell the story in their own words and widens the conversation instead of narrowing it to facts you chose.

options.text: How many presentations do you have this semester?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: Lots of students get nervous. Just practise more and you'll be fine.
options.feedback: False reassurance. Promising it will be fine dismisses the feeling and is a promise you cannot keep. It closes the topic instead of exploring it.

n2.client: It starts the night before. In class my hands shake, I can't breathe properly, and I'm sure everyone can see it. Last week I walked out.

options.text: So you walked out of class.
options.feedback: Simple reflection. Accurate, but it stays at surface level. A complex reflection would add the feeling or meaning and move the session forward.

options.text: Walking out only makes it worse. Next time you must force yourself to stay.
options.feedback: Premature advice (the "righting reflex"). Jumping to solutions before understanding signals you have not heard the client, and it often produces "yes, but..." resistance.

options.text: Part of what's hardest isn't only the racing heart, it's the fear that everyone is watching you fall apart.
options.feedback: Complex reflection (OARS: R). It goes beyond the words to the feeling or meaning underneath. This is Rogers' accurate empathy in action, and it usually deepens the conversation.

n3.client: When I'm up there I think: 'They'll laugh, sir will think I'm stupid, I'll fail the course.'

options.text: That's irrational thinking. Nobody is watching you that closely.
options.feedback: Judgement. Moralising or blaming breaks Rogers' unconditional positive regard and makes further disclosure less likely.

options.text: Let's slow that down. The event is standing up to present, the thought is 'they'll laugh and I'll fail', and the result is the shaking and wanting to escape. Does that fit?
options.feedback: CBT ABC. It separates the Activating event, the Belief or thought, and the emotional or behavioural Consequence, so the client can see the thought as one link in the chain rather than a fact.

options.text: Has anyone actually laughed at you before?
options.feedback: Closed question. Checking the evidence is a useful CBT step later, but asked before the thought is mapped it can sound like you are dismissing her fear.

n4.client: I never thought of the thought being separate. It feels like a fact.

options.text: It makes sense that it feels like a fact. When your body is that alarmed, the mind treats the worry as true.
options.feedback: Validation. It tells the client the reaction makes sense given their situation. This is unconditional positive regard; validating a feeling is not the same as agreeing with every conclusion.

options.text: Thoughts are not facts, that's a basic principle.
options.feedback: Psychoeducation given too early or as a lecture. Accurate, but without first exploring the client's view it lands as a monologue.

options.text: Well, now that you know, just stop believing it.
options.feedback: Premature advice (the "righting reflex"). Jumping to solutions before understanding signals you have not heard the client, and it often produces "yes, but..." resistance.

n5.client: My Abbu says ghabrahat is weakness and I should study more and pray. I do pray. It still happens.

options.text: Does your father know you are here?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: Your father clearly doesn't understand mental health.
options.feedback: Judgement of the family. Criticising a parent pushes the client to defend him and ignores what faith and family may offer her. Stay curious instead.

options.text: You keep going to class, you keep praying, and you came here today even though it was hard. That takes real determination.
options.feedback: Affirmation (OARS: A). It names a genuine strength or effort the client has shown. This builds the alliance and self-efficacy without empty praise.

n6.client: So what do I do before the next one? It's on Thursday.

options.text: Just skip Thursday and ask your teacher for an extension.
options.feedback: Premature advice that also rewards avoidance. Escaping the feared situation brings short-term relief but keeps the fear going.

options.text: Let me pull it together: the panic builds the night before, peaks in class, the thought 'they'll laugh' drives the urge to leave, and you have faith and determination on your side. Shall we plan one small step for Thursday together, like slow breathing and noticing the thought?
options.feedback: Summary (OARS: S). It gathers several threads, shows you have been listening, and lets the client correct or add before you agree a next step together.

options.text: Some people find slow breathing helps. You could try it.
options.feedback: Psychoeducation given too early or as a lecture. Accurate, but without first exploring the client's view it lands as a monologue.

r1.client: I know I should stay. Everyone tells me that. I thought you'd be different.

options.text: Okay. Which subject was the presentation in?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: I'm only telling you what works for anxiety.
options.feedback: Defensiveness after a rupture. The client feels unheard a second time and disengages; the session ends early.

options.text: You're right, I jumped ahead. I'd like to understand what staying in that room feels like for you before suggesting anything.
options.feedback: Rupture repair. Owning the misstep and returning to curiosity restores the alliance; clients notice when a counsellor can admit an error.

supervision: A classic performance-anxiety picture in a capable student. Watch your own righting reflex: the urge to tell her to 'just stay' repeats what everyone else says. Use OARS to map the cycle (anticipation, body alarm, catastrophic thought, escape) and the ABC model to separate the thought from the event. Her faith and her father's expectations are part of her context; work with them, not against them. Graded exposure is a later step, planned with her, not imposed.
referral: Not needed at this stage; counselling with CBT for anxiety is appropriate. Suggest a medical check if physical symptoms occur outside feared situations, and refer to a clinical psychologist if attacks spread beyond presentations or she begins avoiding university.

name: Faraz Qureshi (fictional)
setting: Hyderabad, Sindh (simulated) - urban, Qasimabad; bank officer
presenting: Persistent, hard-to-control worry about money, his children's health and his job, most days for over a year. Poor sleep, muscle tension, irritability and repeated night-time checking of his banking app.
background: Married with two children aged 6 and 3. Grew up in a household that often struggled financially. His wife encouraged him to seek help after he snapped at the children.
culturalNote: Urdu-speaking. As the main earner he feels responsibility for the extended family too. Rising living costs are a real stressor, so avoid implying all his worry is 'irrational'.

n1.client: I worry about everything. Rent, school fees, whether my son's cough is something serious. My wife says I've become a different person.

options.text: How long has this been going on?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: Everyone worries about money these days. Try not to think about it.
options.feedback: False reassurance. Promising it will be fine dismisses the feeling and is a promise you cannot keep. It closes the topic instead of exploring it.

options.text: What's it like for you, carrying all of these worries through a single day?
options.feedback: Open question (OARS: O). It invites the client to tell the story in their own words and widens the conversation instead of narrowing it to facts you chose.

n2.client: Exhausting. At night I check the bank app again and again. I lie awake making lists of what could go wrong.

options.text: Delete the app from your phone and the problem will go away.
options.feedback: Premature advice (the "righting reflex"). Jumping to solutions before understanding signals you have not heard the client, and it often produces "yes, but..." resistance.

options.text: It sounds like worrying has become a kind of duty, as if something bad will slip through the moment you stop checking.
options.feedback: Complex reflection (OARS: R). It goes beyond the words to the feeling or meaning underneath. This is Rogers' accurate empathy in action, and it usually deepens the conversation.

options.text: You check the app a lot at night.
options.feedback: Simple reflection. Accurate, but it stays at surface level. A complex reflection would add the feeling or meaning and move the session forward.

n3.client: If I stop worrying, it feels like I'm being careless with my family.

options.text: So worry has become a way of showing you care. That makes sense, and it's also costing you your sleep and your peace.
options.feedback: Complex reflection (OARS: R). It goes beyond the words to the feeling or meaning underneath. This is Rogers' accurate empathy in action, and it usually deepens the conversation.

options.text: Do you think you are a careless person?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: Worrying never solved anything, you know that.
options.feedback: Judgement. Moralising or blaming breaks Rogers' unconditional positive regard and makes further disclosure less likely.

n4.client: My father struggled with money. I promised myself my children would never go through that.

options.text: Did your father worry a lot too?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: That's in the past. You need to live in the present.
options.feedback: Premature advice (the "righting reflex"). Jumping to solutions before understanding signals you have not heard the client, and it often produces "yes, but..." resistance.

options.text: That promise shows how much you love them. You've built a stable job and a home, which is real evidence of how responsible you are.
options.feedback: Affirmation (OARS: A). It names a genuine strength or effort the client has shown. This builds the alliance and self-efficacy without empty praise.

n5.client: Maybe. But how do I switch it off?

options.text: Once your finances improve, the worry will disappear on its own.
options.feedback: False reassurance. Promising it will be fine dismisses the feeling and is a promise you cannot keep. It closes the topic instead of exploring it.

options.text: Would it be alright if I shared a little about how worry can turn into a habit the mind uses to feel in control? Then you tell me whether it fits your experience.
options.feedback: Collaborative psychoeducation. Brief, plain-language information offered with permission and checked against the client's own experience.

options.text: Have you tried exercise?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

n6.client: That fits too well. I want to try something.

options.text: To summarise: worry about money and the children, night-time checking, a belief that worrying keeps your family safe, and a strong wish to keep your promise. Could we try a set 'worry time' each evening and notice what happens to the checking?
options.feedback: Summary (OARS: S). It gathers several threads, shows you have been listening, and lets the client correct or add before you agree a next step together.

options.text: Worry like yours is common and responds well to therapy.
options.feedback: Psychoeducation given too early or as a lecture. Accurate, but without first exploring the client's view it lands as a monologue.

options.text: You should get sleeping tablets from a doctor.
options.feedback: Premature advice (the "righting reflex"). Jumping to solutions before understanding signals you have not heard the client, and it often produces "yes, but..." resistance.

r1.client: Delete it? I'm a bank officer. That isn't practical.

options.text: If you don't want to change, I can't help you.
options.feedback: Blaming the client for 'resistance' that you created ends the session early. Resistance is often a signal to change your approach.

options.text: Fair point, that suggestion didn't fit your life. Help me understand what checking does for you in the moment.
options.feedback: Rupture repair. Accepting the client's correction and returning to curiosity keeps him engaged.

options.text: Do you check it during the day as well?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

supervision: Worry that is broad, persistent and hard to control, plus tension and poor sleep. Note the function of worry for him: it feels protective. Reflect that function before trying to change it. Checking is a safety behaviour that maintains anxiety. A structured CBT approach (worry time, testing the belief that worry protects) fits once the alliance is built. See DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 for official criteria; do not label him in session.
referral: Counselling is appropriate. Suggest a GP review for sleep and blood pressure. Refer to a clinical psychologist or psychiatrist if worry does not improve with CBT, if low mood deepens, or if he starts using alcohol or sedatives to cope.

name: Ghulam Rasool Jamali (fictional)
setting: Rural Sindh (simulated) - village near Matiari; smallholder farmer
presenting: Months of low mood, poor appetite, early waking, withdrawal from village gatherings and a sense of being a burden after floods destroyed his cotton crop and left him in debt. Discloses passive thoughts of not waking up.
background: Married, five children, two grandchildren. Borrowed from a landlord to replant. His eldest son brought him to the simulated clinic because he has stopped eating properly.
culturalNote: Sindhi-speaking; session supported by a Sindhi-speaking counsellor. Shame in front of other men at the otaq (village sitting place) is central. Faith is a protective factor and his reason against acting on suicidal thoughts. Debt and land are concrete stressors, not just thinking errors.

n1.client: My son brought me. He says I don't eat. What is there to eat for? The water took the cotton, and the debt is still there.

options.text: Insha'Allah next season will be better. Don't lose hope.
options.feedback: False reassurance. Promising it will be fine dismisses the feeling and is a promise you cannot keep. It closes the topic instead of exploring it.

options.text: That is a heavy loss. Would you tell me what these months since the water have been like for you?
options.feedback: Open question (OARS: O). It invites the client to tell the story in their own words and widens the conversation instead of narrowing it to facts you chose.

options.text: How many acres did you lose?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

n2.client: I wake at fajr and just sit. I used to be first in the field. Now I can't face the men at the otaq.

options.text: Losing the crop also took away the man people knew, the one who was first in the field. Facing them now brings shame.
options.feedback: Complex reflection (OARS: R). It goes beyond the words to the feeling or meaning underneath. This is Rogers' accurate empathy in action, and it usually deepens the conversation.

options.text: You don't go to the otaq any more.
options.feedback: Simple reflection. Accurate, but it stays at surface level. A complex reflection would add the feeling or meaning and move the session forward.

options.text: Sitting around won't pay the debt. You have to get up and find work.
options.feedback: Judgement. Moralising or blaming breaks Rogers' unconditional positive regard and makes further disclosure less likely.

n3.client: Sometimes at night I think it would be better if I just didn't wake up. My family would be free of my debt.

options.text: You feel your family would be better off.
options.feedback: Accurate reflection, but it leaves a risk disclosure unexplored. Any hint of wanting to die needs a direct follow-up question about thoughts, plan and intent.

options.text: Don't say such things. You would never do that, you have a family.
options.feedback: False reassurance after a risk disclosure shuts the door. The client learns this topic is not allowed and may not mention it again, which increases risk.

options.text: Thank you for telling me that. I want to ask you plainly, because it matters: when you think about not waking up, have you had thoughts of ending your life, or made any plan?
options.feedback: Calm, direct risk assessment. Asking openly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea; it shows you can hear it and lets you judge risk (thoughts, plan, intent, means) and start safety planning.

n4.client: No plan. I would not do anything; it is haram, and my grandchildren... But the thought comes.

options.text: Good, then there's nothing to worry about. Let's move on.
options.feedback: False reassurance. Promising it will be fine dismisses the feeling and is a promise you cannot keep. It closes the topic instead of exploring it.

options.text: So the thought comes on long nights, there is no plan, and your faith and grandchildren hold you strongly. Can we write down together what helps on those nights, who you can wake, and that you will contact a doctor or a crisis service if the thoughts get stronger?
options.feedback: Summary leading into a safety plan. Naming protective factors, warning signs, people to contact and crisis services in the client's own words is a core step after assessing risk.

options.text: Okay. So you're safe, then?
options.feedback: Closed question that closes the topic too soon. 'No plan' lowers immediate risk but still calls for a written safety plan and follow-up.

n5.client: My son can sit with me. And the pesh imam is a good man; I can speak to him.

options.text: Those are real strengths: a son who brought you here and someone you trust in the community. Reaching out to them is a strong step, not a weak one.
options.feedback: Affirmation (OARS: A). It names a genuine strength or effort the client has shown. This builds the alliance and self-efficacy without empty praise.

options.text: Does the imam know about the debt?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: You should have thought about the debt before borrowing.
options.feedback: Judgement. Moralising or blaming breaks Rogers' unconditional positive regard and makes further disclosure less likely.

n6.client: The doctor at the hospital... will he think I'm mad?

options.text: Depression is very common.
options.feedback: Psychoeducation given too early or as a lecture. Accurate, but without first exploring the client's view it lands as a monologue.

options.text: You don't need a doctor. Just rest and you'll be fine.
options.feedback: False reassurance. Promising it will be fine dismisses the feeling and is a promise you cannot keep. It closes the topic instead of exploring it.

options.text: No. Low mood after a loss like yours is a health problem that doctors treat. I'd like to refer you to the psychiatrist at the clinic for an assessment, give your son the crisis numbers, and see you again this week. Is that alright with you?
options.feedback: Referral handled collaboratively. You explain why, check the client's concerns, and keep the relationship going rather than handing the client off.

r1.client: You sound like the landlord.

options.text: I'm sorry. That came out like blame, and you've had enough of that. I want to understand, not push.
options.feedback: Rupture repair. Apologising for a judgemental remark and returning to empathy is essential, especially with a low-mood client who already feels like a failure.

options.text: Do you still work for the landlord?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: I'm only being realistic.
options.feedback: Defending a judgemental remark confirms the client's shame. With a possible risk case, losing engagement is serious; the session ends early.

supervision: This is a risk case. Low mood after a real economic and identity loss, a sense of being a burden, and passive ideation. Your priorities are engagement, a direct risk assessment, a collaborative safety plan, and referral. Do not let the practical debt problem pull you into advice or blame. Use his faith, his son and the imam as protective resources. Record the risk assessment and inform your supervisor the same day.
referral: Refer for psychiatric assessment of depression. Complete and document a risk assessment and safety plan, involve a trusted family member with consent, and give crisis-service information (see the in-game crisis card). If thoughts become active, or a plan or intent appears, arrange same-day emergency assessment. Signpost debt or flood-relief advice services for the practical stressor.

name: Mehwish Ansari (fictional)
setting: Hyderabad, Sindh (simulated) - urban, Hirabad; homemaker
presenting: Low mood, tearfulness, loss of interest, poor concentration and guilt about 'not being a good mother' since the birth of her second child five months ago. Sleep is broken by the baby and by rumination.
background: Married, lives with husband and in-laws. A trained schoolteacher who stopped working after her first child. Her sister noticed she had stopped calling and brought her in.
culturalNote: Urdu-speaking. Family expects new mothers to be grateful and joyful; low mood after childbirth may be dismissed as 'weakness' or the evil eye (nazar). Normalising without minimising helps reduce shame.

n1.client: Everyone says I should be happy. Two healthy children, a good home. But I just cry when no one's looking.

options.text: What is it like, feeling one way inside while everyone expects you to feel another?
options.feedback: Open question (OARS: O). It invites the client to tell the story in their own words and widens the conversation instead of narrowing it to facts you chose.

options.text: Are you sleeping?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: You should be grateful, many women would love what you have.
options.feedback: Judgement. Moralising or blaming breaks Rogers' unconditional positive regard and makes further disclosure less likely.

n2.client: Lonely. My saas says it's nazar. My husband says I'm tired. Maybe they're right.

options.text: They think it's nazar or tiredness.
options.feedback: Simple reflection. Accurate, but it stays at surface level. A complex reflection would add the feeling or meaning and move the session forward.

options.text: That's superstition. Ignore your mother-in-law.
options.feedback: Judgement. Moralising or blaming breaks Rogers' unconditional positive regard and makes further disclosure less likely.

options.text: Everyone has an explanation, but nobody has asked you what you think is going on.
options.feedback: Complex reflection (OARS: R). It goes beyond the words to the feeling or meaning underneath. This is Rogers' accurate empathy in action, and it usually deepens the conversation.

n3.client: I think I'm a bad mother. When the baby cries I feel nothing, and then I feel terrible for feeling nothing.

options.text: Every mother feels like that. It will pass soon.
options.feedback: False reassurance. Promising it will be fine dismisses the feeling and is a promise you cannot keep. It closes the topic instead of exploring it.

options.text: The baby cries, the thought 'I'm a bad mother' comes, and then guilt piles on top of the numbness. It's a heavy cycle, and it makes sense that you're worn down by it.
options.feedback: CBT ABC. It separates the Activating event, the Belief or thought, and the emotional or behavioural Consequence, so the client can see the thought as one link in the chain rather than a fact.

options.text: How often does the baby wake at night?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

n4.client: I've never told anyone that. Not even my sister.

options.text: It took courage to say it out loud here. That honesty tells me how much you want to be well for your children.
options.feedback: Affirmation (OARS: A). It names a genuine strength or effort the client has shown. This builds the alliance and self-efficacy without empty praise.

options.text: Why haven't you told your sister?
options.feedback: Closed 'why' question. 'Why' can sound like an accusation; reflecting the courage of the disclosure would build more safety.

options.text: You should tell her right away.
options.feedback: Premature advice (the "righting reflex"). Jumping to solutions before understanding signals you have not heard the client, and it often produces "yes, but..." resistance.

n5.client: Do you think something is wrong with me?

options.text: I can't say. Let's keep talking.
options.feedback: Avoiding the question. A brief, collaborative explanation would reduce shame without diagnosing.

options.text: No, you're just tired. Sleep more and it'll lift.
options.feedback: False reassurance. Promising it will be fine dismisses the feeling and is a promise you cannot keep. It closes the topic instead of exploring it.

options.text: Low mood after having a baby is common and treatable, and it's not a sign of being a bad mother. Would it help if I explained a little about it, and you tell me what fits?
options.feedback: Collaborative psychoeducation. Brief, plain-language information offered with permission and checked against the client's own experience.

n6.client: I'd like to feel like myself again. I used to love teaching.

options.feedback: Premature advice (the "righting reflex"). Jumping to solutions before understanding signals you have not heard the client, and it often produces "yes, but..." resistance.

options.text: So we've heard about the tears you hide, the guilt about the baby, everyone's different explanations, and a teacher who misses herself. Would you be open to a doctor's check-up and coming back next week so we can plan small steps together?
options.feedback: Summary (OARS: S). It gathers several threads, shows you have been listening, and lets the client correct or add before you agree a next step together.

options.text: You can go back to teaching later.
options.feedback: Simple reflection. Accurate, but it stays at surface level. A complex reflection would add the feeling or meaning and move the session forward.

r1.client: I didn't say she's superstitious. She's been good to me.

options.text: Okay. Does she help with the baby?
options.feedback: Closed question. It gets a fact but shuts down elaboration. Useful sparingly; here an open question would invite more of the client's story.

options.text: I'm just saying nazar isn't a real thing.
options.feedback: Arguing about the family's beliefs moves the session away from the client and ends engagement.

options.text: You're right, I spoke too quickly. It sounds like you care about her even though her explanation doesn't quite fit.
options.feedback: Rupture repair. Owning the judgement and reflecting her loyalty restores trust.

supervision: Low mood with guilt and numbness in the months after childbirth. Respect the family's explanations while gently making room for the client's own. Screen for thoughts of self-harm and of harm to the baby in a calm, routine way at a later point; she has denied ideation (PHQ-9 item 9 = 0) but re-check. Involve a medical review, since sleep loss, thyroid and anaemia can contribute.
referral: Refer to a GP or obstetric team for a physical review and to a psychiatrist or perinatal mental-health service if symptoms persist or worsen. Urgent same-day referral if she reports thoughts of harming herself or the baby, or any confusion or unusual beliefs; give crisis-service information.

supervision: A referral case. name: Hira Baig (fictional)
setting: Hyderabad, Sindh (simulated) - urban, Latifabad; software tester at a local company
presenting: Anxiety, sleeplessness and conflict with her parents over pressure to accept a marriage proposal from a cousin. She wants to continue her career and choose her own partner, and fears damaging her relationship with her parents.
background: Youngest of four; elder sisters married within the family. Parents are loving but worried about 'what people will say' as she gets older. She financially contributes to the household.
culturalNote: Urdu-speaking. Arranged and cousin marriages are common and often consensual; the issue here is pressure versus her consent, not arranged marriage itself. Family honour and daughters' age at marriage are powerful pressures. Forced marriage is illegal and if coercion or threats appear, protection pathways apply.

supervision: Marriage pressure and the tension between family duty and personal autonomy. Avoid imposing either a 'just comply' or a 'just leave' view.
